items.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 24, 2021 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: before joining the Dizzy Gillespie band I had auditioned to be Mongo Santamaria’s drummer

ctx.x: That’s terrific. And the first gig with Dizzy, just before you told that story you had said with all the other things, you need a little bit of luck and I think you had it.

Oh yes, oh yes. Could you imagine all the names, the drummer’s names Dizzy Gillespie had in his book? And he started calling people [gap] were busy. I could have been busy that night playing a little gig somewhere. And it happens that I was at my aunt’s apartment in the Bronx doing nothing that day. So it was meant to be. It is luck. I always tell people Dizzy and I would have crossed paths anyway because before joining the Dizzy Gillespie band I had auditioned to be Mongo Santamaria’s drummer. So I would run…
Who was it that you replaced? I’m trying to remember.

items.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: It’s not like the Latin jazz of Mongo Santamaria or Ray Barretto or Tito Puente.

ctx.x: All right. Well you’ve been able to get out of the box on the projects you’ve done. And the one you sent me, “Straight Ahead from Havana,” when I listen to it I’m fascinated by the compositions for one thing, and how interactive the whole trio is with all the accents and the, it’s complex. And you’re right there with all of that. You’re very active on this record, and I’m not sure if I have a question here except that I admire it and it’s wonderful music.

Thank you very much, Monk. Thank you, thank you very much. I really appreciate that. My intention with that album was just to do something different. The reason why straight ahead, that’s the music of my passion, straight ahead jazz. So I wanted to do a straight ahead jazz album but I didn’t want to play the tunes that most of jazz players play on a © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

regular basis. The standards. So what I did is I took ten Cuban tunes from a Cuban era that was called the Golden Era of Cuban Music, the Golden Era of Cuban Music, and I took ten old Cuban tunes and gave to them the straight ahead jazz treatment. And also on the album I think there’s like two tunes that we played what people call Latin jazz, but the approach, it is Latin jazz but it’s not the regular Latin jazz that most people know. It’s not like the Latin jazz of Mongo Santamaria or Ray Barretto or Tito…
